literal: 'heroic' Śaiva; by the tradition's derivation, one who delights (ram) in the knowledge (vī) of Śiva–jīva oneness

definitions.definition: Those who delight in the knowledge that awakens the oneness of Śiva and the jīva (SSM 5.15–16); the name of the tradition as a whole and the preferred self-designation of its Pañcācārya strand.
A member of the community that wears the personal liṅga; the preferred name of the Basava-centred strand, some of whose writers distinguish it from 'Vīraśaiva' while others treat the two as synonyms.

One who delights in Śiva-knowledge and keeps māyā away (SSM 5.17–18); in SSM 5.20–21 the Māheśvaras are those devoted to outer worship (the sacrifice of action), not ultimately different from the Śaivas who worship within.
Designation used in an early-twentieth-century printed series of Sanskrit Vīraśaiva texts (the 'Vīraśaiva-liṅgi-brāhmaṇa-dharma-granthamālā') presenting Vīraśaiva dharma in brāhmaṇical terms.

notes: Evidence: series titles on the Muktabodha e-texts M00602, M00612, M00620; relevant to dsp:lingayata-hindu-identity.

definitions.definition: Śiva himself as the unlimited, eternal brahman in which the world dissolves (laya) and from which it arises again, delimited by his own māyā for the sake of worship (SSM 6.36–38); the liṅga is Paraśiva and its pedestal Śakti, their union the universe (11.32); worn on the body as the iṣṭaliṅga.

The gross liṅga given by the guru at initiation and worn outwardly on the body for life (SSM 6.49–50), worshipped on the palm (6.54–55) without invocation or dismissal because Śiva abides in it from the moment of initiation (10.44–47).

equivalents.note: both name the devotee's own chosen form of the divine; the iṣṭaliṅga is a physical sacrament worn on the body, which the iṣṭa-devatā need not be

definitions.definition: The subtle liṅga, made of inner contemplation (SSM 6.49–50): the light that arises from the navel-bulb when prāṇa and apāna meet, in which breath dissolves like frost in the sun (12.6–8); the initiation formula also calls the given liṅga 'your prāṇaliṅga, to be borne like your breath' (6.26).

equivalents.note: internal equivalence within the SSM: the inner liṅga is described as the liṅga of light (6.35; 12.6–9)

literal: the liṅga of feeling / of pure being

definitions.definition: The liṅga in which feeling (bhāva) itself dissolves, grasped by devotion and worshipped with flowers of feeling, superior to liṅgas of clay or stone (SSM 15.37–44); in the vacana triad iṣṭa–prāṇa–bhāva the third, beyond form.

notes: SSM 6.49–50 names the third liṅga of the triad tṛptiliṅga.

definitions.definition: The third, 'beyond the highest' (parātpara) liṅga of the SSM's triad, after the gross iṣṭaliṅga and the subtle prāṇaliṅga.
The supreme liṅga identical with supreme brahman (SSM 12.21–24; 12.38–41); in the ṣaṭsthala correspondences the liṅga of the aikya stage.
One of the six liṅgas of the ṣaṭsthala correspondences — the form of Śiva met at the bhakta stage (vacana and later ṣaṭsthala manuals; the scheme is not set out in these terms in the SSM).
One of the six liṅgas of the ṣaṭsthala correspondences — the form of Śiva met at the māheśvara stage (vacana and later ṣaṭsthala manuals; the scheme is not set out in these terms in the SSM).
One of the six liṅgas of the ṣaṭsthala correspondences — the form of Śiva met at the prasādi stage (vacana and later ṣaṭsthala manuals; the scheme is not set out in these terms in the SSM).
One of the six liṅgas of the ṣaṭsthala correspondences — the form of Śiva met at the prāṇaliṅgi stage (vacana and later ṣaṭsthala manuals; the scheme is not set out in these terms in the SSM).
One of the six liṅgas of the ṣaṭsthala correspondences — the form of Śiva met at the śaraṇa stage (vacana and later ṣaṭsthala manuals; the scheme is not set out in these terms in the SSM).

In the SSM, the liṅga of light that always shines in the base, the heart and between the brows of all beings, called brahman in the Āgamas, contemplated as the inner wearing of the liṅga (6.35; 6.39–41).

notes: Distinct from, though related to, the Purāṇic usage for the twelve self-manifest liṅga shrines.

definitions.definition: An installed liṅga of a temple or shrine; the SSM forbids Vīraśaivas to use its nirmālya but bids them protect such liṅgas even at the cost of life (9.33–35).
The fixed and built — temple, image, installed liṅga — which in Basava's vacana 'shall perish', against the moving (jaṅgama) that endures.

(1) The living, moving devotee or body as Śiva's true temple, against the fixed (Basava's vacana); (2) the wandering Śivayogin teacher whose greatness is taught in the prasādi-sthala — to see him gives accomplishment, to worship him is a means of liberation (SSM 11.37–43); (3) the order of Liṅgāyata priests and monks.

The soul or devotee in relation to the liṅga: knowledge is the aṅga and the eternal knowable the liṅga, and the aṅgaliṅgī has the liṅga mounted on the aṅga and the aṅga present in the liṅga (SSM 12.42–44); the jīva is a part of Śiva through beginningless ignorance (5.34–36).

literal: equal flavour of liṅga and aṅga

definitions.definition: The goal of the path: the soul (aṅga) and Śiva (liṅga) in a union of equal flavour, 'like water poured into water' in common exposition; in the SSM, contemplation of the self dissolved in the sky of consciousness by the nature of sāmarasya (14.42–44).

Union in which the self is contemplated as dissolved in the stainless sky of consciousness; this is the supreme knowledge called liberation (SSM 14.42–44). In the six-bhakti scheme the devotion of the aikya stage is samarasa-bhakti.

notes: Shared term with Nāth and Kashmir Śaiva usage; not asserted equivalent here.

definitions.definition: A station of the path defined by its dharma and its qualified aspirant; the Vīraśaivas are sixfold by the sthalas (SSM 5.22–23), elaborated as 101 sthalas (1.28–31).

notes: The derivation of 'sthala' as that in which all things abide (sthā) and dissolve (la) is common in later exposition; not verified in the SSM here.

definitions.definition: The six stages bhakta, māheśvara, prasādi, prāṇaliṅgi, śaraṇa and aikya (SSM 5.22–23; 5.26; 10.2–3; 11.2; 12.2–3; 13.2; 14.2).
The SSM's elaboration of the path into 101 sthalas — 44 on the side of the soul (aṅga) and 57 on the side of the liṅga — from piṇḍa to jñānaśūnya (1.28–31; 15.1–3).
The first sthala: one in whom devotion to Śiva has arisen; its dharma is taught in fifteen sub-sthalas (SSM 5.26–30).
The second sthala: the bhakta in whom devotion rises through dispassion to steady discernment, steadfast in the liṅga even at the loss of life (SSM 10.2–3; 10.21–22).
The third sthala: one whose bonds of sin are destroyed through steadfastness in the liṅga and who attains serenity of mind through receiving Śiva's grace (SSM 11.2).

literal: one who has the liṅga in the breath

definitions.definition: The fourth sthala, where the yoga of knowledge begins: one who knows the liṅga as consciousness-brahman whose power is the breath (SSM 12.2–3).

literal: refuge; one who has taken refuge

definitions.definition: The fifth sthala: the aṅgaliṅgī as wife and Śiva as husband, possessed of the bliss of their union (SSM 13.2); also the name of the twelfth-century devotees of Kalyāṇa (fem. śaraṇe).
The sixth sthala: free of longing for the droplets of sense-pleasure, pure of intent, immersed in the ocean of Śiva's bliss (SSM 14.2; 14.4); in common usage also the devotee's death (liṅgaikya).
The soul at the stages of bhakta and māheśvara, in the vacana and manual scheme correlated with the gross body and the iṣṭaliṅga.
The soul at the stages of prasādi and prāṇaliṅgi, correlated with the subtle body and the prāṇaliṅga.
The soul at the stages of śaraṇa and aikya, correlated with the causal body and the bhāvaliṅga.
In the six-bhakti scheme of the vacana and manual tradition, the devotion characteristic of the bhakta stage. In the SSM's inner worship faith is the incense (12.13–20).
In the six-bhakti scheme of the vacana and manual tradition, the devotion characteristic of the māheśvara stage. The SSM's māheśvara is marked by steadfastness in the liṅga (liṅganiṣṭhā, 10.21–22).
In the six-bhakti scheme of the vacana and manual tradition, the devotion characteristic of the prasādi stage.

In the six-bhakti scheme of the vacana and manual tradition, the devotion characteristic of the prāṇaliṅgi stage. More widely, lived experience of Śiva — the authority the śaraṇas appeal to, which gave the Anubhava Maṇṭapa its name.
In the six-bhakti scheme of the vacana and manual tradition, the devotion characteristic of the śaraṇa stage. In the SSM the śaraṇa is one possessed of the bliss of union with Śiva (13.2).

'Gu' is what is beyond the qualities and 'ru' what is beyond form; the guru gives that (SSM 15.8–9); Śiva stands present as the guru and the two are not to be distinguished (11.19–21); without devotion to the guru no devotion to Śiva arises (11.22–24).

That by which supreme knowledge is given (dī) and the bondage of fetters destroyed (kṣī) (SSM 15.7); in Vīraśaiva practice the liṅga-initiation, with bathing, the whispered five-syllable mantra and the giving of the liṅga into the disciple's hand (6.19–25); by it the duality of guru and disciple is removed (19.6–7).

notes: The vacana and manual tradition speak of three modes (by touch, by mantra, by rite: vedhā, mantra, kriyā) — moderate confidence.

definitions.definition: The eight protections of the Liṅgāyata: guru, liṅga, jaṅgama, pādōdaka, prasāda, vibhūti, rudrākṣa and mantra; several appear as sub-sthalas of the bhakta-sthala in the SSM (5.27–30).
The five codes: liṅgācāra, sadācāra, śivācāra, bhṛtyācāra and gaṇācāra.
Exclusive worship of Śiva in the liṅga; the SSM forbids worshipping, remembering or praising other gods (9.30–32).
Honest livelihood (kāyaka) and moral life, the fruit of which is shared (dāsōha).
Regarding all Śiva's devotees as equal irrespective of birth.
Humility — the attitude of a servant toward Śiva and his devotees (dāsōhaṃ).

Defence of the faith and the devotees against insult and harm; the SSM bids the devotee protect liṅgas and devotees even at the cost of life and, on meeting a reviler of Śiva, to have him killed, curse him or leave (9.33–36).

Water sanctified by washing the feet of the guru or jaṅgama, received as one of the eight shields; the SSM also reads it as the oneness of guru ('foot') and disciple ('water') through initiation (19.6–7).

Purity of mind achieved by Śiva's grace; whatever is offered to Śiva is his prasāda, and eating only what has been offered purifies the mind (SSM 11.2; 11.6–11); devotion and grace arise from each other like seed and sprout (9.11–12).
What has been offered to Śiva, which purifies the mind (SSM 11.6–11); the nirmālya of fixed (temple) liṅgas is not to be used by Vīraśaivas (9.33–35).
Holy ash, one of the eight shields; called vibhūti because it causes prosperity (SSM 7.4–5).
Ash, so called because it reproaches sins; bathing in ash is the supreme 'fire-bath' (SSM 7.4–5; 7.23–25).
The three horizontal lines of ash on the forehead and body; the SSM's qualified guru is eager to wear it (6.1–6).
The seed-beads born from Śiva's tears at the burning of the Triple City (SSM 7.47–48), one of the eight shields; wearing them frees brāhmaṇa and outcaste alike (7.62).

The mantra 'namaḥ śivāya', designation of Śiva and root of all mantras, at the head of all the śrutis; there is no mantra greater (SSM 8.2–7); whispered into the disciple's right ear at initiation (6.19–21).
'Oṃ namaḥ śivāya', in which Śiva who is both partless (revealed by Oṃ) and with parts (revealed by the five syllables) abides (SSM 8.17–22).
The single syllable that reveals the partless, second-less Śiva; it arises from 'so'ham' by dropping the 'h' and the 's' (SSM 8.17–22).
In the SSM the mantra of the supreme self (8.17–22) and the feeling with which the haṃsa-formed supreme self is contemplated in śivayoga-samādhi (12.21–24).
In Basava's vacana the stance the devotee asks to be spared ('do not make me say sōhaṃ'), in favour of dāsōhaṃ, 'I am your servant'.

(1) The devotee's self-understanding as servant of Śiva and his devotees, which Basava asks for in place of 'I am He'; (2) the giving of the fruits of one's work (kāyaka) to the jaṅgamas and the community, and in later usage free communal feeding.

equivalents.note: dāsōha includes service but also names the servant-stance and the sharing of earned wealth

definitions.definition: Honest work in one's occupation undertaken as worship; 'work is Kailāsa' (Āydakki Mārayya's vacana), not to be interrupted even for the guru, the liṅga or a jaṅgama, and not to gather more than the day's need.

equivalents.note: both make work an offering; kāyaka is specifically one's livelihood, with its fruit shared (dāsōha)

definitions.definition: In Allama Prabhu's teaching the void in which liṅga, aṅga and all attainments are no longer two; the 'attainment of the void' gives the Śūnyasampādane its name.

equivalents.note: Allama's śūnya is Śiva's own void-fullness (liṅga as bayalu); interpreters in the tradition reject its identification with Buddhist emptiness, though the word is shared

definitions.definition: Allama's Kannada word for the void — open space without enclosure — in which the devotee, the liṅga and the world disappear.

equivalents.note: Kannada and Sanskrit words used side by side for the void in Allama's vacanas

definitions.definition: The seat of the presiding master of the Anubhava Maṇṭapa, occupied by Allama Prabhu in the Śūnyasampādane.
The assembly at Kalyāṇa where, in the tradition's account, the śaraṇas of every birth and both sexes discussed their experience of Śiva under Allama's presidency.
Direct experience of Śiva; the SSM's author is named Śivayogi from his experience of Śiva in the supreme sky of consciousness-bliss (1.13–24).
A short rhythmic Kannada prose-poem spoken from experience, usually closing with the author's signature name for the Lord; the scripture of the śaraṇa strand.
The signature name for the Lord that closes a vacanakāra's vacanas — Kūḍalasaṅgamadēva (Basava), Guhēśvara (Allama), Cennamallikārjuna (Akka), Rāmanātha (Dāsimayya) — usually received from the guru.
An author of vacanas.
The enigmatic, paradoxical vacanas (beḍagina vacana) especially of Allama Prabhu.
Later Vīraśaiva devotional songs composed for singing, as distinct from the prose-rhythm vacanas.
The ancient Śaiva saints, above all the Tamil Nāyaṉmārs, whose lives Vīraśaiva hagiography narrates as models for the śaraṇas.
A non-initiate or one averse to the conduct of the path; the SSM bids the devotee refuse goods sent by bhavis (9.30–32).
Offering to the liṅga everything meant for one's own enjoyment before enjoying it, so that all is received as prasāda (SSM 11.6–11).
The small casket in which the iṣṭaliṅga is worn on a cord at the chest or neck.
Bearing the liṅga, outwardly on the body and inwardly in the mind; the given liṅga is never to be separated from the body (SSM 6.26; 6.30–33; 6.48).
The palm of the hand as the seat on which the iṣṭaliṅga is worshipped, better than an outer pedestal (SSM 6.54–55).
Contemplation of Śiva as the self through inner worship of the prāṇaliṅga, culminating in samādhi (SSM 12.21–24); those who see the world as consciousness through it are Śivayogins (11.37–43).

equivalents.note: Vīraśaiva yoga is directed to the liṅga and includes liṅga-gazing and inner worship

definitions.definition: One who sees the world as consciousness through Śiva-yoga, has conquered desire and anger, and is equal to clod and gold, friend and foe (SSM 11.37–43).
The celibate renunciant order of Liṅgāyata maṭhas, associated with the Basava-centred tradition and the lineage of Toṇṭada Siddhaliṅga.

equivalents.note: renunciant life within a liṅga-wearing, non-Vedic-sannyāsa order

definitions.definition: The five seats founded by the five ācāryas — Rambhāpurī, Ujjayinī, Kedāra, Śrīśaila and Kāśī.
Ritual impurity; the teacher who has become Śiva is not tainted by it (SSM 14.16); the vacana tradition rejects such pollution for all liṅga-wearers.
The five kinds of pollution the Liṅgāyatas reject: of birth, of death, of menstruation, of leftovers (ucchiṣṭa) and of caste (jāti).

notes: Membership of the list from memory; verify.

definitions.definition: The SSM tells the māheśvara to give up the dharmas of his jāti and family that oppose steadfastness in the liṅga (10.30–31), yet prescribes commensality with twice-born of one's own jāti on the path (9.29), and makes brāhmaṇa and outcaste alike for those in the contemplation of Śiva (14.19–20).
The vacanas reject caste among devotees: Basava calls himself the son in the house of the cobbler Mādāra Cennayya and asks to say of every devotee 'he is ours'.
Impurity binding the soul; Śiva is so called because he is free of the three impurities (SSM 8.8–11); in union the bond of impurity is shaken off (14.5–7).
The impurity by whose contact the self, resting in the inner organ, has become atomic (aṇu) (SSM 18.5–7).

Śiva's power through which he takes names and forms (SSM 1.9) and by whose concealment difference in Śiva is imagined (14.8–9); the Vīramāheśvara keeps it away (5.17–18). Allama: gold, woman and land are not māyā — the desire before the mind is.
The guṇa of darkness: one who hates all people, always makes 'I' and holds untrue notions is tāmasa, and its removal by the guru is a sub-stage of the śaraṇa (SSM 13.17–19).

Śambhu, dense with consciousness and bliss, so called because pure from the beginning, free of the three impurities and the abode of all auspiciousness; the two syllables reveal supreme brahman in their primary sense (SSM 8.8–11); the ocean of consciousness whose waves are the thirty-six tattvas (1.3).
Śiva as the liṅga itself, with the supreme Śakti as its pedestal (SSM 11.32).
Śiva's power: the pedestal of the liṅga (SSM 11.32), the breath as the liṅga's power (12.2–3), the great power named Umā that lights the supreme self (12.21–24).

Devotion to Śiva, ninefold (SSM 9.2–3), outer and inner (9.6–9), arising from grace and giving rise to grace (9.11–12); its presence, not birth, makes one a bhakta (9.4–5); in the six-bhakti scheme it rises from faith to samarasa.
One whose mind is settled that the liṅga is liberation itself is liberated even while embodied (SSM 12.46); the liṅga-sthalas are directed to it (15.1–3).
The upsurge of Śiva's bliss in the Śivayogin in whom the world has dissolved (SSM 14.15); the supreme knowledge of the self dissolved in sāmarasya (14.42–44).

Rejected as a practice for the worshipper at the māheśvara stage, since worship rests on difference (SSM 10.37–43), and affirmed at the aikya stage, where difference is seen to be imagined by māyā (14.8–14).
The SSM's name for its own doctrine: the śāstra devoted to Śiva's non-duality agreeing with Veda and Vedānta (3.83–87), taught by gurus devoted to Śiva-non-duality (13.24–27).

The philosophical name of Vīraśaiva doctrine in Śrīpati's Śrīkarabhāṣya (philosophy owned by U16); the SSM's teaching that the liṅga is Śiva with Śakti as its pedestal and the universe their union (11.32) is its root image.
Mahādeva as the Lord on whom the bound soul depends (SSM 10.40); at union lordship and boundness are seen as imagined by māyā (14.8–9).
The soul dependent on the Lord, its servant at the stage of practice (SSM 10.40); 'who is paśu, who pati?' when māyā dissolves (14.8–9).

literal: the relation of wife and husband

definitions.definition: The śaraṇa as wife (satī) and Śiva as husband (pati), the bliss of their union defining the śaraṇa-sthala (SSM 13.2; 13.5–7); lived in Akka Mahādēvi's vacanas; in the Kannada maxim, 'the śaraṇa is the wife, the liṅga the husband'.

equivalents.note: bridal devotion to the Lord in both; the Vīraśaiva form is tied to a named sthala of the ṣaṭsthala path

definitions.definition: The aikya sub-stage in which, contemplating the universe as made of Śiva, one's self is the single vessel of Śiva (SSM 14.28–33).
The aikya sub-stage in which guru, Śiva and disciple are remembered as one's own nature (SSM 14.34–36).
The knowledge 'I am Śiva, I am the guru, I am the whole world' (SSM 14.38–41).
Earth and the other elements, sun, moon and the self as Śiva's eight forms — in the SSM his body and effect, over which he presides, neither non-different from him nor separate (10.48–52).
Inviting the deity into an image for worship; not done for the iṣṭaliṅga, in which Śiva already abides from initiation (SSM 10.44–47).
Śiva's attendants — the pramathas such as Reṇuka and Dāruka (SSM 2.25–27; 3.67–77) — and by extension the community of devotees whose defence is gaṇācāra.
Beings emitted by Śiva, equal to him in splendour and able to create and dissolve worlds, among them Reṇuka and Dāruka (SSM 2.25–27).
Union with the liṅga — the aikya stage, and in common usage the death of a devotee, who is buried rather than cremated.
The thirty-six principles, which are the waves and bubbles of Śiva as the ocean of consciousness (SSM 1.3).

A part of the formless Śiva through connection with beginningless ignorance, in whom Śiva abides as fire in the sunstone (SSM 5.34–36); at the prāṇaliṅgi stage the breath is the jīva and the great liṅga brahman (12.21–24).

The eternal self, distinct from body, senses and intellect, known through the I-cognition and memory (SSM 5.55–60); dwelling in the heart like the hundredth part of a hair-tip, shining like a lamp (18.5–7).
The liṅga itself, so named for its vastness and expanding (SSM 6.36–38); the liṅga of light by whose light all shines (12.38–41).
The attainment of meditation on Śiva as the self through inner worship; undivided attention on the haṃsa-formed supreme self contemplated as 'I am He' (SSM 12.21–24).
The first sub-sthala: the embodied soul made fit for the path by the ripening of karma and Śiva's grace (SSM 5.27–30; cf. 5.34–36).
Discernment of the self as distinct from body, senses and intellect, and of the Lord as distinct from the selves (SSM 5.55–60).
One who has taken the higher way of Śiva-worship and resorts again to lower practice (SSM 9.39–40).
Inquiry into Śiva's principle; steady feeling in Śiva; single steadfastness in Śiva-knowledge, like a faithful wife's conduct (SSM 13.30–36).
The liṅga-sthala where action dissolves through the guru's knowledge; all rites are a fraction of liṅga-worship (SSM 15.30–36).
The liṅga-sthala in which the knowledge that makes feeling known itself dissolves; brahman beyond the three forms and the three qualities (SSM 15.45–49, not separately recorded as a teaching here).
